title: What Moses wrote of the making of the world
source_text: Οὔπω δὲ λέγω ὅτι, εἴπερ ὑπέμεινε καὶ ἠνέσχετο ἐπακοῦσαι τῶν, ὥς φησι, συγγραμμάτων Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν, ἐπέστησεν ἂν, τί δήποτε τὸ μὲν „ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς“ ἐπ᾿ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς τέτακται καὶ τοῦ καλουμένου στερεώματος ἔτι δὲ καὶ φωστήρων καὶ ἀστέρων καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ἐπὶ κητῶν μεγάλων καὶ πάσης ψυχῆς „ζῴων ἑρπετῶν, ἃ ἐξήγαγε τὰ ὕδατα κατὰ γένη αὐτῶν,“ καὶ παντὸς πετεινοῦ πτερωτοῦ „κατὰ γένος“ καὶ ἑξῆς τούτοις ἐπὶ τῶν θηρίων „τῆς γῆς κατὰ γένος“ καὶ τῶν κτηνῶν „κατὰ γένος“ καὶ πάντων τῶν ἑρπετῶν „τῆς γῆς κατὰ γένος“ αὐτῶν καὶ τελευταῖον ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. μὴ εἰρημένου δὲ τοῦ „ἐποίησε“ περὶ ἑτέρων. ἀρκεῖται ὁ λόγος περὶ φωτὸς μὲν τῷ „ἐγένετο φῶς“ ἐπὶ δὲ συναγωγῆς μιᾶς παντὸς ὕδατος τοῦ ὑποκάτω παντὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ τῷ „ἐγένετο οὕτως“· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν βλαστησάντων ἀπὸ γῆς, ὅτ᾿ „ἐξήνεγκεν ἡ γῆ βοτάνην χόρτου σπεῖρον σπέρμα κατὰ γένος καὶ καθ᾿ ὁμοιότητα καὶ ξύλον κάρπιμον ποιοῦν καρπὸν, οὗ τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ κατὰ γένος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.“ καὶ ἐζήτησεν ἂν, εἰ αἱ γεγραμμέναι προστάξεις τοῦ θεοῦ περὶ τοῦ γενέσθαι ἕκαστον τοῦ κόσμου μέρος τίνι ἢ τίσιν εἴρηνται, καὶ οὐκ ἂν εὐχερῶς κατηγόρησεν ὡς ἀδιανοήτων καὶ μηδεμίαν σύνεσιν ἀπόῤῥητον ἐχόντων τῶν ἢ ὑπὸ Μωϋσέως ἐν τούτοις γεγραμμένων ἢ, ὡς ἡμεῖς εἴποιμεν ἂν, ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐν Μωϋσεῖ θείου πνεύματος, ἀφ᾿ οὗ καὶ ἐπροφήτευσεν· ἐπεὶ μᾶλλον ᾔδει τά τ᾿ ἐόντα τά τ᾿ ἐσσόμενα πρό τ᾿ ἐόντα τῶν λεγομένων παρὰ τοῖς ποιηταῖς μάντεων ταῦτ᾿ ἐγνωκέναι.
pass_a_gloss: I do not yet (οὔπω) say that, if he had endured (ὑπομένω) and borne (ἀνέχομαι) to listen (ἐπακούω) to the, as he says, writings (σύγγραμμα) of Moses and the prophets, he would have noticed (ἐφίστημι) why ever (τί δήποτε) 'God made' (ἐποίησεν ὁ θεός) is placed (τάσσω) upon heaven and earth and the so-called firmament (στερέωμα), and further lights (φωστήρ) and stars, and after these upon great sea creatures (κῆτος) and every soul 'of creeping living things which the waters brought out (ἐξάγω) according to their kinds (γένος)', and every winged bird (πετεινὸν πτερωτόν) 'according to kind', and next upon wild beasts (θηρίον) 'of the earth according to kind', and cattle (κτῆνος) 'according to kind', and all creeping things 'of the earth according to their kind', and last upon man. 'Made' not being said about others, the word (λόγος) is content (ἀρκέομαι) about light with 'light came to be' (ἐγένετο φῶς), and upon the gathering (συναγωγή) into one of all the water under the whole heaven with 'it came to be so' (ἐγένετο οὕτως); likewise upon things that sprouted (βλαστάνω) from earth, when 'the earth brought forth (ἐκφέρω) plant of grass (βοτάνη χόρτου) sowing seed according to kind and according to likeness (ὁμοιότης), and fruitful tree (ξύλον κάρπιμον) making fruit whose seed is in it according to kind upon the earth'. And he would have sought whether the written commands (πρόσταξις) of God about the coming-to-be (γίνομαι) of each part of the world were spoken to whom or to whom (pl.), and would not readily (εὐχερῶς) have accused (κατηγορέω) as unintelligible (ἀδιανόητος) and having no secret (ἀπόρρητος) understanding (σύνεσις) the things written in these either by Moses or, as we would say, by the divine Spirit (θεῖον πνεῦμα) in Moses, from whom he also prophesied (προφητεύω); since he knew more (μᾶλλον) 'the things being, those to be, and those before being' than the seers (μάντις) spoken of among the poets to have known these.
pass_b_english: I am not yet saying that, if he had, as he puts it, “been patient and borne to listen to the writings” of Moses and the prophets, he would have noticed why the words “God made” are applied to heaven and earth (Genesis 1:1), and to what is called the firmament (Genesis 1:7), and further to the lights and the stars (Genesis 1:16); after these to the great sea creatures and every soul “of creeping living things, which the waters brought forth according to their kinds,” and every winged bird “according to its kind” (Genesis 1:21); next to the wild beasts “of the earth according to their kind,” and the cattle “according to their kind,” and all the creeping things “of the earth according to their kind” (Genesis 1:25); and last of all to man (Genesis 1:27). But “made” is not said of other things. For light, the text is content with “light came to be” (Genesis 1:3); and for the gathering into one of all the water beneath the whole heaven, with “it was so” (Genesis 1:9). It is the same with the things that sprouted from the earth, when “the earth brought forth plants of grass, sowing seed according to their kind and likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree yielding fruit whose seed is in it, according to its kind, on the earth” (Genesis 1:12).

He would also have asked to whom, whether to one or to more than one, the written commands of God about the coming into being of each part of the world were spoken. And he would not lightly have accused, as unintelligible and holding no hidden meaning, what was written here either by Moses or, as we would say, by the divine Spirit in Moses, by whom he also prophesied. For Moses knew “the things that are, the things that will be, and the things that were before” (Homer, Iliad 1.70) better than the seers whom the poets speak of as having known them.

choices.choice: Οὔπω λέγω: 'I am not yet saying'
echo of Celsus's phrase now includes 'the writings' (ὥς φησι stands beside συγγραμμάτων)
'and' moved out of the quoted ἐγένετο οὕτως
Genesis 1:1, 1:3, 1:7, 1:9, 1:12, 1:16, 1:21, 1:25, 1:27 checked against LXX wording; Iliad 1.70 checked; subject of ᾗδει kept as Moses (could be the Spirit; Greek leaves it open)

The quoted wording agrees with the LXX of Genesis 1:21, 1:25 and 1:12; 'and it was so' (ἐγένετο οὕτως) closes Genesis 1:9. The references for heaven and earth (1:1), the firmament (1:7), the lights and stars (1:16) and man (1:27) mark where the LXX has ἐποίησεν ὁ θεός. 'As he puts it, “been patient and borne to listen to”' takes up Celsus's own phrase in 4.52 (εἴ τις ὑπομείναι καὶ ἀνάσχοιτο αὐτῶν ἐπακοῦσαι τῶν συγγραμμάτων); ὥς φησι stands before συγγραμμάτων in the Greek. 'To whom, whether to one or to more than one' (τίνι ἢ τίσιν) hints at the plural 'Let us make' of Genesis 1:26 without quoting it, so no citation is given. Homer, Iliad 1.70 describes the seer Calchas (ὃς ᾔδη τά τ' ἐόντα τά τ' ἐσσόμενα πρό τ' ἐόντα); Origen applies the line to Moses. The subject of ᾔδει is taken as Moses.
